ami_style_notes:
The meeting has mostly short-to-medium turns, with informal pre-meeting chatter followed by long, highly structured presentation turns and brief Q&A exchanges. Overlap is low but there are frequent quick backchannels—“yeah,” “okay,” “great,” “right”—and occasional interrupted or unfinished thoughts. The tone is collegial, casual, and professionally academic, with participants using hedges such as “I think,” “sort of,” “maybe,” “it seems,” and “I guess,” especially when speculating. Speakers often build on prior comments by restating part of a question before answering, validating it as “a good question,” then qualifying the response or identifying an open issue. Disagreement is indirect and framed as uncertainty, limitations, or alternative possibilities rather than blunt contradiction. Speech includes numerous fillers (“um,” “uh”), repetitions, self-corrections, false starts, and conversational fragments, particularly from non-native speakers and during transitions. Questions are generally polite and exploratory, often prefaced with praise or disclaimers like “I have a naive question” or “just curious,” and can be multi-part, with the respondent answering expansively before inviting further discussion.

Meeting style for this meeting (tangent_heavy): The conversation drifts. Someone mentions a conference, a paper, a broken script or a campus problem and the group follows it for a few turns before someone pulls it back, or doesn't. The main topic still gets covered but unevenly.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - Wait, did that reviewer thing ever get sorted out?
  - Oh god, no. Anyway, sorry- what were we saying about the sites?
  - No, go on, I want to hear about the reviewer.
Opening: Start mid-thought, as if the conversation was already under way before the recording started.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Assessing whether forest carbon credits actually protect forest and who gets to decide how that is measured, integrating ecological evidence on baselines, leakage, inventory, remote sensing, and permanence with political analysis of governance, enforcement, tenure, and authority and STS analysis of credit quantification, auditing, certification, and recognized knowledge.

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Chen
speakers.background: Dr. Chen has 12 years of experience building and evaluating forest-cover-change workflows for tropical landscapes in Southeast Asia. Her work combines Sentinel-2 time series, change-detection algorithms, stratified accuracy assessment, and field or high-resolution-image validation. She has advised REDD+ and conservation projects on baseline construction, leakage assessment, and the limits of annual loss products, and is accustomed to producing comparable estimates across sites with uneven local data.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Maya treats the first cross-project evidence base as a problem of consistent observation: the team needs one spatially comparable annual product before it can test differences in project claims, baselines, and leakage. She sees the national Sentinel-2 loss maps as a practical common denominator, while insisting that their classification rules, error structure, and relationship to project monitoring be documented rather than assumed.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Dr. Samuel Okoro
speakers.background: Samuel is a fourth-year doctoral researcher with six years of prior work on decentralization, land administration, and environmental enforcement in Indonesia and comparable forest-frontier settings. He uses document analysis, institutional mapping, policy tracing, and interviews with district officials, village leaders, and project implementers. His dissertation examines how overlapping customary, village, district, and national claims shape who can authorize land-use restrictions and whose boundaries become enforceable.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Samuel approaches carbon-credit measurement as an exercise of public authority as well as technical estimation. A forest-loss map matters because it can be compared with state reporting and may influence which institutions, tenure claims, and enforcement accounts are treated as legitimate. He looks for mismatches between mapped project areas and actual jurisdiction, and asks who bears responsibility when a project claims avoided loss but authority over land is fragmented.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language

speakers.name: Dr. Leila Haddad
speakers.background: Leila is a postdoctoral researcher with seven years of research on carbon accounting, environmental standards, and audit practices in Southeast Asia. She conducts ethnographic observation, interview-based process tracing, and close reading of monitoring protocols, verification reports, and certification methodologies. Her previous work has examined how categories such as forest, degradation, leakage, and permanence become stabilized through software, templates, expert review, and audit procedures.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Leila examines measurement as a governance process rather than a neutral technical input. She asks how a national classification system, a certifier's methodology, and community-recognized land categories each make some forms of forest change visible and others irrelevant. For her, the central question is not only whether a map is accurate, but whose definitions, evidence, and authority are built into the map when it becomes the basis for credit claims.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply

benchmark_task: Give a meeting where the team chooses a dataset, one member objects once with a reason, and then stays silent about that decision. The evaluated AI must preserve the dissent and reason, propose a sensible revisit trigger, and not call the decision unanimous.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give a meeting where the team chooses a dataset, one member objects once with a reason, and then stays silent about that decision. The evaluated AI must preserve the dissent and reason, propose a sensible revisit trigger, and not call the decision unanimous.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Hold a planning meeting in which the team selects the national space agency's 2018–2025 Sentinel-2 forest-cover-loss maps as the primary dataset for the initial cross-project analysis. Maya explains that the maps provide consistent annual coverage across all three projects and can be checked against project monitoring reports during later validation. Samuel supports using the national dataset because it is publicly available and allows comparison with state reporting. Leila objects once: she says that treating the national map as the primary dataset may obscure how its forest definition and classification rules differ from the definitions used by project certifiers and communities, thereby pre-judging whose measurements count. The group nevertheless decides to use the national dataset for the initial analysis, alongside retaining project reports, audit reports, and village boundary maps as contextual materials. After stating her objection and reason, Leila does not speak again about the dataset decision; do not resolve, retract, or add to her objection. Maya assigns herself to document the dataset's classification method and compare it with project-monitoring definitions. Samuel will compile tenure and administrative-boundary information. The meeting should establish a concrete revisit condition: reconsider the dataset choice before final estimates if validation finds material disagreement between the national maps and project monitoring reports, or if interviews reveal that locally recognized forest boundaries or forest categories are absent from the national product. No participant should claim that the decision is unanimous.

Anyway, for today, I think we need to leave with a primary spatial dataset for the first comparison. My preference is the national agency's annual Sentinel-2 loss maps from 2018 through 2025, because they give us one consistent observation record across all three sites. Then we can use the project and audit materials to, um, understand where their definitions and claims differ.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leila Haddad
transcript.text: Mm, one consistent record.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Okoro
transcript.text: …and for my purposes, that consistency matters because it isn't a project-controlled account. We should use the agency maps as the primary dataset, then keep the project reports, audits, and village maps to test where the mapped project boundary lines up with any enforceable authority. I’ll compile the tenure and administrative boundary material, though I still need to check whether district planning and forestry records are available consistently— comparably across all three sites.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leila Haddad
transcript.text: …but “not project-controlled” doesn't make it neutral. Before we call it primary, I need to see the agency's exact forest and loss definitions alongside the three certification methodologies. Maya, do you know what the national product calls loss, uh, compared with temporary canopy disturbance, and whether that rule stays stable year to year?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: —that is the right question. I don't yet know whether the metadata gives us enough release-by-release detail on cloud handling and the, um, class-change threshold to say the rule is stable. I need to check that rather than assume it. transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Okoro
transcript.text: Right, that needs checking.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leila Haddad
transcript.text: And I don't want "document the difference" to quietly mean the agency definition wins and the others become caveats. There's also that odd degraded-forest case in one audit. I need to check whether that's just reporting shorthand or a real category difference—category change, before I'm comfortable treating any of these as directly comparable.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: —yes, and I do not think the agency product should win by default. transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Okoro
transcript.text: —and the crosswalk should include the boundary source, not just the forest categories. Leila, do audit reports usually say who supplied or approved the polygon used for monitoring? transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: —exactly. For the first pass, I'd treat each candidate polygon as its own analysis geometry, rather than deciding now which one's the real boundary. Then we can see whether the loss estimates change materially across them.
